newsitem.title: UK: British tobacco giant not worried on smoking gun.
newsitem.headline: British tobacco giant not worried on smoking gun.

text.p: British tobacco and insurance group B.A.T Industries Plc , facing a series of U.S. lawsuits, said Thursday that anti-tobacco investigators would fail to unearth any documentary evidence showing it believed cigarettes were addictive.

B.A.T, which controls 17 percent of the U.S. cigarette market, which accounts for 620 billion pounds ($1 billion), or a quarter, of its total profits last year, said a "smoking gun" would not be unearthed in a mountain of documents it has released over the past few years.
"Millions of millions of documents have been made available to the plaintiffs' attorneys in the U.S.," said B.A.T spokesman Ralph Edmondson.
"If there was anything that was relevant, I'm sure the attorneys would have brought it to the public's attention by now. I don't believe there is anything else to emerge."

Edmondson's comments followed news Wednesday that a U.S. federal judge had reinstated an investors' lawsuit against Philip Morris Inc. that claims the world's largest tobacco group hid negative information about smoking from shareholders.

In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs said the company artificially inflated its stock price by maintaining the public stance "that nicotine is not addictive (and) that smoking is entirely a matter of 'choice.'"

U.S. District Judge Michael Mukasey said he had restored the suit, originally dismissed in 1995, due to new evidence that specifically identified Philip Morris and tobacco industry documents discussing studies concerning whether cigarettes and nicotine are additive.

"This new documentary evidence is of enough potential importance and volume that I probably would not have granted a defendants' motion to dismiss had it been described in the initial complaint," Mukasey said.

B.A.T, along with the rest of the tobacco industry, is embroiled in litigation from more than 20 U.S. state attorneys general who are trying to recoup state healthcare funds spent to treat smoking-related illnesses. Alongside the state battles are several separate personal injury suits, as well as a state-by-state collection of private class action suits.
B.A.T is spending $100 million a year on legal fees.
"It's just part of doing business there," Edmondson said. "We believe we will prevail in the various lawsuits we are defending in the U.S."
B.A.T shares have dropped 11 percent since mid-March, when U.S. rival Liggett Group became the first tobacco company to admit smoking was addictive and could cause cancer.

Although B.A.T is confident it will win the legal battles, Chief Executive Martin Broughton said last month that it would be sensible to evaluate any settlement that would cover all current and future claims if approved by Congress and the White House.
